newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope writes to Yeltsin over Russia religious curbs.
newsitem.headline: Pope writes to Yeltsin over Russia religious curbs.

text.p: Pope John Paul has written to President Boris Yeltsin expressing deep concern over a legislative measure to curb the rights of minority religions in Russia, the Vatican said on Thursday.
Deputy Vatican spokesman Father Ciro Benedettini told Reuters that the letter had been written and the Vatican might release the text later on Thursday.
Vatican sources said the Pope, who is vacationing in the northern Italian Alps, expressed concern that Catholicism would suffer discrimination if Yeltsin signed the measure into law.
The measure, passed by the Russian parliament, would deny legal status to new religious groups for 15 years.

It would give higher legal status to those religious organisations that have been in existence in Russia for 50 years, a definition that encompasses the Russian Orthodox Church, Jewish, Islamic and Buddhist groups.
The bill, entitled "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association", would also impose new curbs on religious activities by foreign groups.
Russian human-rights activists have urged Yeltsin to veto the bill, saying it will enflame religious tensions at home.
According to some religious activists opposed to the bill, those who would be stripped of their legal status include Catholics, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Methodists, Baptists, and Adventists.
The Russian Orthodox Church strongly supports the bill.
The U.S. Senate voted earlier this week to cut off aid to Russia if Yeltsin signed the measure.
Relations between the Catholic and the Russian Orthodox Churches are currently at one of their lowest levels ever.
The Orthodox have accused Catholics of using their new-found freedom in the countries of the former Soviet Union to woo converts.

Shortly before an inter-religious conference in Austria last month, Patriarch Alexiy II of the Russian Orthodox Church called off a proposed meeting with the Pope, saying the churches needed to settle several important issues first.
It would have been the first meeting of its kind since the Great Schism split the Christian churches into eastern and western branches in 1054.

Last month, for the first time in 21 years, the Orthodox Church did not send a delegation to an annual feast at the Vatican in representation of Ecumenical Patriarch of Istanbul, spiritual leader of the world's Orthodox Christians.
Better relations with the Orthodox Church would be essential if the Pope is to realise his dream of visiting Moscow to preach reconciliation and Christian unity.
Yeltsin has invited the Pope to visit Russia but the Pontiff cannot make the trip without the green light from the Russian Orthodox Church.
Religion has made a strong comeback in Russia since the collapse of atheistic communism, after which all religions were made equal under the country's post-Soviet constitution.
But the new bill has given rise to fears among human rights activists that Russia might be returning to a kind of Soviet-style repression and discrimination.
